eursta.why: The region's most urban bird, labelled only wetland and shoreline: it never tops the frequency list at a wildlife refuge, and none of the urban anchors is actually a street or a yard.

marwre.why: A cattail-marsh specialist. It reached the list only through the Tillamook Bay salt marsh, so it was tagged shoreline and not wetland.

norpin.why: A dabbling duck of flooded fields and marshes. Wetland's cutoff was the highest of the four, so it was cut there and kept at the coast.

killde.why: Nests on beaches, gravel lots and playing fields, not just wet meadows.

barswa.why: Nests on buildings and bridges and forages over open water and fields; shoreline-only is an artifact of where it happened to rank.

whcspa.why: Abundant in city scrub, parks and yards; the urban anchors are wooded parks where it is scarcer than at the coast.

buffle.why: Winters on ponds, lakes and sloughs as well as salt water.

moudov.why: A bird of yards, wires and open ground. The forest tag comes from the open lawns at Pittock Mansion, not from woodland.

cedwax.why: Roams widely through riparian corridors and woodland edge; urban-only reflects one fruiting-tree hotspot.

yerwar.why: Winters through woodland and willow edge across the region, not only in city parks.

norsho.why: A dabbling duck. The forest tag comes from the ponds inside Tualatin Hills Nature Park.

rewbla.why: A marsh blackbird. Same ponds at Tualatin Hills Nature Park; it does not hold territory in closed-canopy forest.
